subject: 고대의 조선술과 목재 조달
title: Ancient shipbuilding and the timber it demanded
content: A large ancient warship consumed the trunks of many mature trees, and the timber had to meet requirements that ordinary woodland rarely satisfied. Keels needed long straight lengths, frames needed pieces already curved in the grain, and both had to come from species that resisted rot in seawater. Because such trees grew slowly, a fleet represented an accumulation of centuries rather than a season of labour, and this fact shaped where naval powers could arise. The consequences show up in the historical record as dependence. States with harbours but without forests bought their timber abroad, and their naval strength therefore rested on routes that a rival could interrupt. Ancient sources record treaties concerned with access to particular mountainsides, and archaeologists have traced the movement of specific woods across long distances by examining the grain in wrecks. What looks like a purely military history turns out to involve the geography of trees. Exhaustion followed where demand outran growth. Regions that supplied shipyards for generations show pollen records in which the useful species decline and scrub replaces them, and the shipyards that had depended on them either moved or built with inferior wood. Historians accordingly treat ancient naval decline as sometimes an ecological event rather than a military one, since a fleet cannot be rebuilt from forests that no longer exist.

subject: 고대 도시의 화재와 건축 규제
title: Fire and building rules in the ancient city
content: Ancient cities burned frequently, and the reasons were structural rather than accidental. Buildings stood wall to wall, upper storeys were framed in timber, cooking and lighting used open flame, and water arrived in quantities suited to drinking rather than to firefighting. A blaze that began in one workshop could therefore consume a quarter before anyone organized a response, and the archaeological record preserves these episodes as burn layers that seal everything beneath them. What followed such disasters is where the historical interest lies. Ancient authorities responded with rules about height, about the materials permitted in party walls, and about the width of streets, and the surviving texts show these being issued repeatedly. Repetition indicates that enforcement failed, since a rule obeyed once does not need reissuing, and the economic reason is plain enough. Building in stone cost more than building in timber, and a landlord letting rooms to tenants had little incentive to bear the difference. The regulations therefore record a conflict rather than a solution. Where they did take hold, it was usually after a fire large enough to destroy the interests that had resisted them, and the rebuilt quarters show the new standards while older districts nearby retain the old. Historians read that contrast in the excavated plan as evidence of when the balance of interests shifted.

subject: 고대의 우편과 봉인
title: Ancient letters and the seals that closed them
content: Writing a message solves only half of a problem, because the recipient must also know that what arrived is what was sent. Ancient administrations addressed this with seals, pressing a carved stone into clay or wax so that the closure could not be opened without destroying the impression. Thousands of such seals and sealings survive, and they tell historians a good deal that the letters themselves omit. The impressions record who had authority to close a document, and their distribution across a site shows where correspondence was received and stored. Because a seal was personal and difficult to copy, it also functioned as a signature, and disputes recorded in ancient legal texts turn on whether a particular impression was genuine. What the system could not do was keep the contents private from the carrier, since a messenger who wished to read a tablet could break the clay and claim it had been damaged. Ancient correspondence therefore relied on trusted couriers as much as on seals, and the most sensitive matters were often not written at all. Instructions survive telling a messenger to deliver part of the message from memory, which means the written portion was deliberately incomplete. Historians reading such letters must therefore treat them as fragments of an exchange whose most important content was spoken.

subject: 고대 아메리카의 옥수수 재배 확산
title: The spread of maize through ancient America
content: Maize was developed from a wild grass whose seed head looks almost nothing like a modern cob, and the change took thousands of years of selection by farmers who could not have known where it would lead. Excavated sites preserve the intermediate stages, with cobs from later centuries growing longer while their kernels lose the hard casing that had protected them in the wild. Each step made the plant more useful to people and less able to survive without them. Moving it northward took more than carrying seed. Maize responds to day length, so varieties suited to one latitude flower at the wrong time when shifted, and the plant had to be reselected as it travelled. The long pauses in the record match these adjustments rather than any break in contact, and its arrival in the north stands as an agricultural feat as large as the original domestication. What came after that arrival was social as much as agricultural. Communities that had combined foraging with small gardens now built their year around a crop that rewarded stored surplus and concentrated settlement, and the ancient towns of those regions appear soon afterward. Historians therefore treat the northward spread of maize as a condition for the societies that later occupied those valleys.

subject: 고대 지중해의 난파선이 말하는 교역
title: What ancient shipwrecks reveal about trade
content: A wreck on the seabed preserves a cargo as it was loaded, which written sources almost never do, and underwater archaeology has therefore changed what historians believe about ancient commerce. Ledgers record what merchants chose to write down, whereas a sunken hull holds everything that was aboard, including the goods too ordinary to mention and the personal possessions of the crew. Several assumptions have not survived this evidence. Cargoes turn out to be mixed rather than uniform, with amphorae from several regions stowed together, which indicates that ships called at many ports and traded in small quantities rather than carrying a single consignment between two cities. The presence of goods from beyond the recorded trading world shows connections that the ancient texts do not mention at all. Dating the wrecks has produced a further result. Their frequency across the centuries rises and falls, and the pattern tracks other indicators of ancient economic activity closely enough that historians use it as a proxy for the volume of Mediterranean shipping. That the proxy exists at all is an accident of preservation, since only vessels that sank leave this kind of record. Corrections for the routes most likely to produce wrecks are therefore necessary, and the resulting curve remains one of the few quantitative series available for the ancient economy.

subject: 고대 인더스의 도장과 교역 표식
title: Seals and trade marks of the ancient Indus
content: The cities of the ancient Indus valley produced thousands of small carved seals, each bearing an animal figure and a short sequence of signs, and these objects are among the most informative artefacts the civilization left. They were pressed into clay to close containers and to label goods, so their find spots trace where sealed consignments travelled. Examples recovered far to the west, in the cities of Mesopotamia, establish a commercial connection that no text from either side describes in detail. What the seals cannot yet tell us is what they say, since the script remains undeciphered and the inscriptions are too short for the statistical methods that have cracked other ancient writing systems. Scholars nonetheless extract information from their structure. Sign sequences repeat in ways that suggest names or titles, particular animals cluster in particular quarters of a city, and the combination of a figure with a sign group behaves like a mark of ownership or origin. The absence of decipherment therefore limits but does not prevent historical inference. Trade routes, administrative organization, and the standardization of weights can all be established from where the seals occur and how they were used, and these conclusions rest on archaeology rather than on reading. Historians of the ancient Indus accordingly work from material evidence in a way that historians of neighbouring civilizations rarely need to.

subject: 중세 이슬람의 관개와 작물 전파
title: Medieval irrigation and the crops it carried
content: A group of crops moved westward across the medieval Islamic world, among them sugar cane, rice, citrus, and cotton, and their spread reshaped farming in regions where they had been unknown. What made the movement possible was not merely the carrying of seed, since these plants require summer water in landscapes whose rain falls in winter. Their arrival therefore rested on watering methods that travelled with them. Those methods were varied and adapted to each locality. Buried channels drew water from hill springs with little loss to evaporation, wheels raised it from rivers to fields above, and cisterns held winter rain for summer use. Each demanded upkeep that a single household could not provide, so the crops arrived embedded in rules for shared labour and for dividing water among users, and medieval legal texts devote many pages to those rules. The agricultural gains were substantial. Summer cropping on land that had lain fallow raised yields, and the new plants supported industries in sugar and textiles that changed what regions exported. Historians argue about how rapid the change was and how much of it preceded the medieval period, and that argument turns on dating evidence which is often thin. What nobody disputes is that crops and the means of watering them travelled together, since neither would have worked alone.

subject: 초기 근대의 인구 조사와 국가
title: Counting people and the making of the state
content: Rulers have always wanted to know how many subjects they had, and yet sound head counts are fairly recent, because the earlier tries measured something else. Medieval and early modern surveys counted hearths, taxed households, or men owing service, and each of those units answered a question of office rather than of numbers. Turning them into people takes guesses that historians argue over without end. What changed in the early modern period was the point of counting. Rulers began to treat the people themselves as a resource to be handled rather than as a base to be taxed, and this shift yielded registers that noted births and deaths as they came instead of listing houses now and then. Parishes kept the new records and later offices took them over, and their survival gives us a run of years where before there had been only snapshots. Counting also changed what it found. A household that knew it was being listed for the army had reason to hide its young men, and a village taxed as a whole had reason to say it was smaller, so the records show dodging as much as they show numbers. Historians thus read early counts beside the motives that surrounded them, and the fixes applied are often larger than what the counts were meant to reveal.

subject: 중세 유럽의 시장 특허와 도시 성장
title: Market charters and the growth of medieval towns
content: A medieval market did not simply happen where people wished to trade, because holding one required a grant from a lord or a king, and the documents recording these grants survive in large numbers. Each specified the days on which trading was permitted, the dues that would be collected, and often the distance within which no rival market might be established. The grant was therefore a monopoly as much as a permission. What the holder gained was revenue, and what the traders gained was protection. A market under charter offered a court that would hear disputes arising within it, weights that had been checked, and a guarantee of safe passage on the days it was held, and these were conditions that unregulated exchange could not supply. Merchants accordingly travelled to chartered markets even when nearer opportunities existed, which is why the grants were worth paying for. The pattern of charters therefore maps the growth of medieval commerce with unusual precision. Clusters appear where routes crossed, gaps appear where an existing holder had blocked competition, and the dates show trade expanding through the twelfth and thirteenth centuries before contracting after the epidemics of the fourteenth. Historians use the series as evidence about the economy precisely because the documents were produced for reasons that had nothing to do with recording it.

subject: 고대 근동의 조약과 외교 언어
title: Treaties and the language of ancient diplomacy
content: Ancient states in the Near East concluded treaties with one another, and enough of these documents survive on clay to show that a shared diplomatic form developed across the region. The texts open by naming the parties and rehearsing their past dealings, set out obligations, and close by calling the gods of both sides to witness, and this structure recurs across centuries and across languages. Its persistence indicates that scribes were trained in a common tradition. What the form accomplished was enforcement in the absence of any authority above the parties. A treaty could not be upheld by a court, so it was bound instead by oaths whose violation invited divine punishment, and the lists of witnessing gods were correspondingly long and carefully balanced between the two sides. The curses attached to breach are the most elaborate sections of many tablets, which reflects where the drafters thought the difficulty lay. Correspondence between courts used the same conventions and often the same language, so that rulers wrote to one another in a tongue native to neither. Historians read this shared medium as evidence of a diplomatic system rather than a series of bilateral encounters, since a common form implies common training, regular contact, and expectations that both sides understood before negotiation began.

subject: 아프리카 사바나의 야금과 교역
title: Metalworking and exchange in the African savanna
content: Ironworking began early across much of Africa, and the furnaces dug up in savanna lands show ways of working that differ sharply from those used elsewhere. Tall shaft furnaces drew air by draught rather than by bellows, reaching heats that yielded good metal in one go, and the slag heaps beside them show work going on at some sites for many centuries. That scale points to output well beyond local need. What the surplus fed was trade with lands that had no ore. Iron tools moved outward along roads that also carried salt, cloth, and copper, and the villages at the crossings of those roads grew into towns whose wealth rested on goods passing through. Because ironworking ate charcoal in bulk, the trade also thinned the woods around the furnaces, and pollen cores record that loss. Smiths held a place apart in many of these societies, at times honoured and at times shunned, and oral accounts gathered much later tell of their standing. Historians weigh those accounts with care while noting that the dug evidence fits a picture of a skilled group whose craft passed within families. What the furnaces show on their own is that the method was worked out on the spot rather than brought from outside, which older accounts had simply assumed.

subject: 중세 몽골 이후의 교역 재편
title: Trade after the medieval Mongol peace
content: For roughly a century the overland routes across medieval Asia lay under a single authority, and merchants could travel from the Mediterranean to China with documents that officials along the way would honour. Travellers of the period describe the journey as arduous but feasible, and the goods, techniques, and reports that moved in those decades altered every region they touched. What came afterward is described less often and matters just as much. When that authority fragmented, the routes did not simply close, because trade continued under the states that followed and each taxed its own stretch. The cumulative burden rose, safety became uncertain, and the epidemics of the period discouraged travel further. Merchants responded by turning to the sea, where a single ship could carry what a caravan could not and where fewer powers demanded payment. The maritime routes had always existed, and they now absorbed traffic that had gone overland. The consequences fell unevenly. Inland cities that had grown on the caravan trade declined, while ports on the southern seas expanded, and the political weight of the regions shifted with them. Historians therefore read the later medieval search for sea passages as the continuation of a movement already under way rather than as a sudden departure, since the traffic had been leaving the land routes for generations.
